## What it is

The World Health Organization issued its first guidelines on the diagnosis and management of type 1 diabetes in adults on 14 November 2026, marking World Diabetes Day, with recommendations designed for all settings, including low-resource, emergency and humanitarian ones (World Health Organization [WHO], 2026b). The 125-page document strongly recommends intensified insulin therapy, which means multiple daily injections with doses adjusted to blood glucose values. It allows either human insulin or insulin analogues, while preferring human insulin because of its generally lower cost (WHO, 2026a). A published summary reports 14 recommendations, one strong and thirteen conditional, with a glycated haemoglobin target of 7% or lower (53 mmol/mol) for most adults and a suggestion to consider islet autoantibody and C-peptide testing where the diagnosis is uncertain (Jha, 2026).

## Why it matters

Type 1 diabetes is often seen as a childhood condition. WHO estimates that 9.5 million people lived with it in 2025, with a further 500,000 diagnosed that year, and it is increasingly affecting adults (WHO, 2026b). For Zambia the diagnostic gap is the first concern, as the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) estimates 750,400 adults aged 20 to 79 years with diabetes in 2024, an age-standardised prevalence of 10.3%, which ranks third in the African region, and 86.0% of those adults undiagnosed (IDF, 2025). Those figures cover all types of diabetes, most of which is type 2 (WHO, 2026b), so they give no type 1 count. They do show how limited detection is in a setting where adults with type 1 diabetes are sometimes misclassified as type 2, particularly where diagnostic tools and specialist care are scarce, and where delayed diagnosis raises the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (Jha, 2026).

## What to remember

We should read the document first as an insulin guideline, since its title and overview centre on insulin use. Thirteen of the fourteen recommendations are conditional, so local resources and patient preferences should shape the regimen chosen (WHO, 2026a; Jha, 2026). Human insulin remains an appropriate and effective option. Glucose monitoring may use finger-prick tests or continuous glucose monitors, with urine glucose testing as a fallback where blood testing is unavailable (WHO, 2026b). The recommendations set a clinical standard but do not themselves secure supply, so the practical question for Zambia is whether insulin, test strips and glycated haemoglobin testing reach the facilities where adults present, which these sources do not address.
